module_title: Block Making Materials and Mix Ratios

lessons.title: Standard mix ratios for common block types
lessons.body: When making blocks, the mix ratio is the amount of cement compared to the amount of sand and aggregate. In Africa, we usually measure by volume using buckets or wheelbarrows. The most common mix for solid load-bearing blocks is 1:5: meaning one part cement to five parts sand. For hollow blocks that are not load-bearing, you can use 1:6 or even 1:7. The ratio changes based on the strength you need. For a 9-inch solid block that will carry heavy walls, use 1:5. For a 6-inch hollow block for a fence, 1:6 is fine. Never go weaker than 1:7 for any block that will be exposed to weather. A common mistake is to add more sand to save cement. That makes weak blocks that crack and crumble. If you are making blocks for a foundation, use 1:4 or 1:5. For a single-storey house wall, 1:5 or 1:6. For a garden wall, 1:6 or 1:7. Remember, the ratio is by volume, not weight. So if you use one bucket of cement, you need five buckets of sand. But sand must be clean and free of clay or roots. If the sand is dirty, wash it or use more cement. In many parts of Africa, people use a wheelbarrow as the measure. One wheelbarrow of cement to five wheelbarrows of sand is too much cement; that is 1:5 but a wheelbarrow is large. Better to use smaller containers like buckets for accuracy. Always mix on a clean concrete floor or metal sheet. Never mix on bare ground because soil will contaminate the mix. Start by measuring sand first, then add cement on top. Mix dry until the colour is uniform. Then add water slowly. The mix should be stiff, not runny. A good test: squeeze a handful; it should hold shape without dripping water. If it drips, too wet. If it crumbles, too dry. Adjust with small amounts. These ratios work for most common blocks in Africa, but always test a few blocks first and let them cure for 7 days before using them in a wall.

lessons.title: Measuring materials without a weighing scale: using buckets and wheelbarrows
lessons.body: Most block makers in Africa don't have a weighing scale. That's fine. You can measure accurately with buckets, wheelbarrows, or even tins. The key is to use the same container for all measurements. A standard 20-litre bucket is common. For a 1:5 mix, you need 1 bucket of cement to 5 buckets of sand. But cement is often sold in 50kg bags. One 50kg bag of cement is about 33 litres by volume. So if you use a 20-litre bucket, one bag fills about 1.5 buckets. That means for a 1:5 mix, you would need 1.5 buckets of cement to 7.5 buckets of sand. But that's awkward. Better to use a smaller container, like a 10-litre bucket. Then one 50kg bag is about 3.3 buckets of cement. For 1:5, you need 3.3 buckets cement to 16.5 buckets sand. Still not round. Many block makers use a wheelbarrow as the main measure. A standard wheelbarrow holds about 60 litres. One bag of cement is about half a wheelbarrow. So for 1:5, you need half a wheelbarrow of cement to 2.5 wheelbarrows of sand. That's easy: 1 bag cement to 2.5 wheelbarrows sand. But wheelbarrows vary in size. So always check your own wheelbarrow. Fill it with water using a bucket to know its volume. Then you can calculate. Another method: use a wooden box. Make a box 30cm x 30cm x 30cm. That is 27 litres. One bag of cement is about 1.2 boxes. For 1:5, use 1.2 boxes cement to 6 boxes sand. The most important rule: never guess. Always use the same container for cement and sand. If you use a bucket for cement, use the same bucket for sand. Level off each bucket with a straight stick. Don't heap it. A heaped bucket has more material. Also, remember that sand is often wet. Wet sand takes more volume. So if sand is wet, use slightly less sand or add a little more cement. In the rainy season, sand can be soaked. Then you might need to adjust. But for dry sand, the bucket method works well. Practice with a small batch first. Make 10 blocks with your measurements. If they are strong after 7 days, your measurements are good. If they crack, add more cement. This is how you learn without a scale.

lessons.title: Adding water: how much is too much or too little
lessons.body: Water is the most common mistake in block making. Too much water makes weak, porous blocks that crack and shrink. Too little water makes a crumbly mix that won't hold shape. The right amount of water is about 5 to 7 litres per 50kg bag of cement for a 1:5 mix. But that depends on how wet your sand is. If your sand is dry, you might need 7 litres. If it's already damp, maybe 4 litres. Never just pour water from a hose. Use a bucket or watering can so you can control it. Add water slowly while mixing. The mix should be stiff, like thick porridge, not runny like soup. A good test: pick up a handful and squeeze. It should form a ball that holds together without dripping water. When you open your hand, the ball should stay intact. If water drips out, it's too wet. If it crumbles, it's too dry. Another test: drop the ball from knee height. It should flatten slightly but not splash. For block making, you want a mix that is drier than for concrete slabs. Blocks need to hold their shape immediately after pressing. If the mix is too wet, the block will sag and lose shape. If it's too dry, the block will have holes and weak edges. In hot African climates, water evaporates fast. So mix only as much as you can use in 30 minutes. If you leave the mix sitting, it will dry out. You can add a little water and remix, but never add water to a mix that has already started to set. That is dangerous. Also, use clean water. Dirty water with oil, salt, or organic matter will weaken the cement. In many rural areas, people use water from rivers or wells. That's fine if it's clear. But if it's muddy, let it settle and use the clear part. Never use seawater for reinforced blocks because salt rusts steel, but for plain blocks, seawater can be used in small amounts, though it may cause efflorescence (white stains). Best to use fresh water. Remember, the goal is a mix that is workable but stiff. Practice with small batches. If you can't shape a block that stands on its own without slumping, it's too wet. If the block crumbles when you touch it, it's too dry. Adjust by adding small amounts of water or dry cement and sand.

lessons.title: Using admixtures and waterproofers in rainy seasons
lessons.body: In the rainy season, block making becomes difficult. Too much moisture in the air and in the sand can ruin your blocks. Admixtures are chemicals you add to the mix to improve properties. Waterproofers are a type of admixture that makes blocks repel water. In Africa, you can buy liquid waterproofers at hardware stores. Common brands include Sika, Fosroc, or local equivalents. They are added at about 0.5 to 1 litre per 50kg bag of cement. For rainy season, a waterproofer helps blocks resist water penetration, reducing dampness and efflorescence. Another useful admixture is a plasticiser, which makes the mix more workable with less water. That means you can use a stiffer mix without adding too much water. This is great for block making because stiff mixes produce stronger blocks. A plasticiser is added at about 0.2 to 0.5 litres per bag. If you can't afford admixtures, you can use alternative methods. For example, add a small amount of lime (about 5% of cement weight) to improve workability and water resistance. Or use wood ash, but that reduces strength. In the rainy season, your sand will be wet. That means you must reduce the water you add. Test the sand first: squeeze a handful. If it drips, it's too wet. Spread it out to dry for a few hours before mixing. Also, cover your blocks with plastic sheets or tarpaulins after casting. Rain can erode fresh blocks. Cure them under cover for at least 7 days. If you must make blocks in the rain, work under a shed. Use a waterproofer to help the blocks shed water. But remember, admixtures are not a substitute for good mix ratios. You still need the right cement-to-sand ratio. Also, never mix admixtures with bare hands; use gloves. Store them away from children. In the dry season, you may not need waterproofers. But in the rainy season, they are worth the extra cost. They can reduce block breakage and improve durability. If you are making blocks for a foundation in a wet area, always use a waterproofer. It will save you money in the long run.

lessons.title: Mixing small batches by hand on a clean surface
lessons.body: For small-scale block making, you don't need a mixer. You can mix by hand on a clean, flat surface. This is how most blocks are made in Africa. First, choose a clean concrete floor or a metal sheet. Never mix on bare ground because soil will get into the mix and weaken it. If you must mix on ground, first lay a tarpaulin or plastic sheet. The surface should be hard and smooth. Start by measuring your sand. For a 1:5 mix, measure 5 buckets of sand. Spread it in a ring or a flat layer. Then measure 1 bucket of cement. Pour the cement on top of the sand. Now, using a shovel or hoe, mix the dry materials. Stand on one side and pull the sand and cement towards you, turning it over. Keep turning until the colour is uniform. There should be no streaks of brown sand or grey cement. This takes about 3 to 5 minutes. Next, make a crater in the middle of the dry mix. Pour water into the crater. Add water slowly. Start with about 4 litres for a 1:5 mix using one bag of cement. Then use your shovel to fold the dry mix into the water. Keep turning and folding. Add more water if needed, but a little at a time. The mix should become stiff but uniform. If you add too much water, you cannot remove it. So be careful. Once the mix is ready, use it within 30 minutes. If it starts to dry, you can add a tiny bit of water and remix, but never add water to a mix that has begun to set. After mixing, clean your surface immediately. Dried cement is hard to remove. For small batches, you can mix with a hoe in a wheelbarrow. That is even easier. Put sand and cement in the wheelbarrow, mix dry, then add water and mix with a hoe. This is good for making 10 to 20 blocks at a time. Always wear gloves and a dust mask when handling cement. Cement dust is harmful to your lungs. Also, work in a shaded area if possible. The sun can dry the mix too fast. With practice, you can mix a batch in 10 minutes. Remember, consistency is key. Use the same method every time so your blocks are uniform.

lessons.title: Calculating how many blocks one bag of cement can make
lessons.body: One of the most common questions is: how many blocks can I make with one bag of cement? The answer depends on the block size, mix ratio, and how much sand you use. Let's take a standard 9-inch solid block (450mm x 225mm x 225mm). Its volume is about 0.0228 cubic metres. For a 1:5 mix, the total volume of cement and sand needed for one block is about 0.0228 cubic metres. But cement is only 1/6 of that volume (since 1 part cement to 5 parts sand = 6 parts total). So cement volume per block = 0.0228 / 6 = 0.0038 cubic metres. One 50kg bag of cement has a volume of about 0.033 cubic metres (33 litres). So number of blocks per bag = 0.033 / 0.0038 = about 8.7 blocks. So you get about 8 to 9 solid 9-inch blocks per bag of cement. For a 6-inch hollow block (400mm x 200mm x 150mm), the volume is about 0.012 cubic metres. But hollow blocks have voids, so the actual material volume is less. Typically, a 6-inch hollow block uses about 0.008 cubic metres of mix. For 1:6 mix, cement volume per block = 0.008 / 7 = 0.00114 cubic metres. Blocks per bag = 0.033 / 0.00114 = about 29 blocks. So one bag can make about 25 to 30 hollow 6-inch blocks. For a 4-inch solid block (400mm x 200mm x 100mm), volume = 0.008 cubic metres. For 1:5 mix, cement volume = 0.008 / 6 = 0.00133 cubic metres. Blocks per bag = 0.033 / 0.00133 = about 25 blocks. So one bag makes about 25 solid 4-inch blocks. These numbers are estimates. Your actual yield depends on how well you measure and how much waste you have. Also, if you use a richer mix (1:4), you get fewer blocks per bag. If you use a leaner mix (1:7), you get more blocks but they are weaker. Always test a small batch to find your actual yield. For example, make 10 blocks and see how much cement you used. Then calculate. Keep a record. In Africa, many block makers sell blocks by the bag of cement. They know that one bag makes about 8 solid 9-inch blocks. So they price accordingly. If you are making blocks for a project, calculate the total number of blocks needed, then divide by the yield per bag to know how many bags to buy. Always add 5% extra for waste. Also, remember that the sand quality affects yield. Dirty sand needs more cement. So always use clean sand.

quiz.q: What is the most common mix ratio for solid load-bearing blocks?
quiz.explanation: 1:5 is the standard mix for solid load-bearing blocks because it provides good strength.

quiz.q: Which mix ratio is suitable for a garden wall?
quiz.explanation: Garden walls do not carry heavy loads, so a leaner mix like 1:6 or 1:7 is sufficient.

quiz.q: What is the volume of a standard 50kg bag of cement?
quiz.explanation: A 50kg bag of cement has a volume of about 33 litres.

quiz.q: When measuring without a scale, why should you use the same container for cement and sand?
quiz.explanation: Using the same container ensures the ratio is by volume and accurate.

quiz.q: What is a good test to check if the mix has the right amount of water?
options: A) It should drip water when squeezed
B) It should crumble when squeezed
C) It should hold shape without dripping
D) It should flow like soup
quiz.explanation: A correct mix holds its shape when squeezed and does not drip water.

quiz.q: Why is it bad to add too much water to a block mix?
options: A) It makes the mix stronger
B) It makes blocks weak and porous
C) It makes blocks cure faster
D) It reduces the need for cement
quiz.explanation: Excess water creates voids and weakens the block, leading to cracks.

quiz.q: What is a waterproofer admixture used for?
options: B) To make blocks repel water
quiz.explanation: Waterproofers reduce water penetration, which is useful in rainy seasons.

quiz.q: How much waterproofer is typically added per 50kg bag of cement?
quiz.explanation: Waterproofers are added at about 0.5 to 1 litre per bag of cement.

quiz.q: What should you do if your sand is wet in the rainy season?
options: C) Reduce the water you add
quiz.explanation: Wet sand already contains water, so you need to add less water to the mix.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix on bare ground?
quiz.explanation: Soil gets into the mix and weakens the blocks.

quiz.q: What is the first step when mixing by hand?
options: B) Mix dry sand and cement
quiz.explanation: You must first mix the dry materials until uniform before adding water.

quiz.q: How long should you mix a small batch by hand?
quiz.explanation: Mixing dry materials for 3 to 5 minutes ensures uniform colour and consistency.

quiz.q: How many solid 9-inch blocks can one bag of cement make approximately?
quiz.explanation: Based on volume calculations, one bag makes about 8 to 9 solid 9-inch blocks.

quiz.q: How many 6-inch hollow blocks can one bag of cement make approximately?
quiz.explanation: Hollow blocks use less material, so one bag can make about 25 to 30 blocks.

quiz.q: What is the volume of a standard 9-inch solid block?
quiz.explanation: A 9-inch solid block (450x225x225mm) has a volume of about 0.0228 mÂ³.

quiz.q: Why should you add 5% extra cement when calculating bags for a project?
quiz.explanation: Extra cement covers waste, spillage, and slight variations in mix.

quiz.q: What is a plasticiser used for in block making?
options: B) To improve workability with less water
quiz.explanation: Plasticisers make the mix more workable without adding extra water, improving strength.

quiz.q: What is a common local alternative to admixtures for water resistance?
quiz.explanation: Lime can be added (about 5% of cement weight) to improve workability and water resistance.

quiz.q: Why should you cover fresh blocks in the rainy season?
options: C) To make them cure faster
D) To hide them from thieves
quiz.explanation: Rain can erode fresh blocks, so covering them with plastic sheets protects them.

quiz.q: What is the correct water-to-cement ratio for a 1:5 mix using dry sand?
quiz.explanation: About 5 to 7 litres of water per 50kg bag is typical for a 1:5 mix with dry sand.

quiz.q: What happens if you add water to a mix that has already started to set?
options: D) It makes the mix last longer
quiz.explanation: Adding water after setting begins disrupts the chemical reaction and weakens the block.

quiz.q: Why is clean water important for block making?
options: C) Clean water is easier to find
D) Dirty water makes blocks heavier
quiz.explanation: Impurities like oil, salt, or organic matter can interfere with cement hydration and weaken blocks.

quiz.q: What is the best surface for hand mixing?
options: C) Clean concrete floor or metal sheet
quiz.explanation: A clean, hard surface prevents soil contamination and makes mixing easier.

quiz.q: How can you check the volume of your wheelbarrow?
options: B) Fill with water using a bucket
quiz.explanation: Filling with water using a known bucket gives an accurate volume measurement.

quiz.q: What is the danger of using a heaped bucket instead of a level one?
options: B) It changes the mix ratio
quiz.explanation: A heaped bucket contains more material, so the ratio becomes inaccurate.

quiz.q: Why should you wear a dust mask when mixing cement?
options: B) Cement dust is harmful to lungs
quiz.explanation: Cement dust can cause respiratory problems, so a mask is essential.

quiz.q: What is the approximate volume of a 6-inch hollow block?
quiz.explanation: A 6-inch hollow block (400x200x150mm) has a volume of about 0.012 mÂ³.

quiz.q: Why might you need to add more cement if your sand is dirty?
options: B) Dirty sand weakens the mix
quiz.explanation: Clay and silt in dirty sand reduce bond strength, so more cement is needed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended curing time for blocks before use?
quiz.explanation: Blocks should cure for at least 7 days to gain sufficient strength for handling.

quiz.q: How many solid 4-inch blocks can one bag of cement make approximately?
quiz.explanation: One bag makes about 25 solid 4-inch blocks with a 1:5 mix.
